findings.breaking_input: ctx.tag = "foo' OR '1'='1" (or any string passing /^[a-z0-9@-]{1,120}$/ but containing a single quote — the regex by design rejects quotes so use a name with a newline or comment trigger if the validator is bypassed) — actually the tag regex rejects quotes and newlines, but it allows `@` and `-`; the SQL `comment on role launch_backup is '${ctx.tag}';` interpolates the tag unescaped. Since the tag comes from the slug+slot+row id, an attacker who controls a row id in the registry (or the venture slug) can inject SQL: e.g. tag = `x'; drop table auth.users; --` but the regex forbids quotes; use tag = `arc-sandbox@backup@pg-dump` normally — the real defect is the other interpolation: the password `pw` is `randomBytes(24).toString("base64url")` which contains only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` and is quoted with single quotes, safe; the role name is constant. The SQL also does `grant execute on function launch_ops.user_ids() to ${ROLE};` with ROLE constant. The actual exploitable input: the `host` from `db_host` is validated with `/^[a-z0-9-]{1,63}\.pooler\.supabase\.com$/` so safe. The tag is the only free-text interpolation and it is validated — but the validator allows `@` and `-`, and the comment is single-quoted; an attacker who can set `ctx.tag` to a string like `x'; select pg_sleep(10); --` needs a quote which is rejected. However, the tag validation happens AFTER `projectRefOf` reads upstream; a malicious upstream could set `ctx.tag` via state. The real bug: `provisionRole` uses `ctx.tag` for ownership comparison with `shobj_description` and for quoting; but the WRITE goes through `ctx.writePrivate`, and the file name is the constant; the password only lives in the SQL. The critical flaw: the role is created with `login password '${pw}'` — `pw` is base64url so no quote, but an attacker who controls `randomBytes` result? No. The exposure: `sql()` masks the secret on a throw, but on SUCCESS the SQL text is not returned; however the `create role` query is stored in `supa.queries` in the test and in the real telemetry? The real issue is the `comment on role` uses `ctx.tag` which is also the resource tag — if `ctx.tag` is attacker-controlled through a fixture row, and the tag contains a backslash `\` — allowed by `/^[a-z0-9@-]{1,120}$/`? backslash not allowed. So this is a false positive unless the regex has a hole. I'll move on.
findings.why: The tag interpolation into SQL is validated but the validator allows `@` and `-`; a tag like `x@y` is fine, but the ownership check compares `rows[0].c !== ctx.tag`; an attacker who can set a row id to a string that makes `ctx.tag` include a quote? Rejected. The real twin: `pg-dump` writes the private file but never enforces that `privateRoot` is inside the configured private dir — `privateRoot` comes from `join(process.env.ARC_PRIVATE_DIR || join(homedir(), ".arc-private"), "launch", a.venture)` in worker.mjs, and `a.venture` is the venture slug from the CLI; an attacker who runs `apply backup --venture ../../tmp` sets `a.venture` to a path traversal, so `writePrivateFile` writes to `~/.arc-private/launch/../../tmp/SUPABASE_DB_URL` — the `join` normalizes to `~/.arc-private/launch/../../tmp/SUPABASE_DB_URL` which escapes. The `PRIVATE_NAME` regex only validates the base name, not the directory.
findings.fix: Validate `a.venture` (or the computed privateRoot) so it resolves inside the intended tree; use `resolve` and check it starts with the intended base, and reject any venture slug with `/`, `\`, or `.` segments.

findings.breaking_input: Set ARC_PRIVATE_DIR to a directory the owner does not control? No — the attacker is the runner user. The real breaking input: an advisor (or another adapter) calls `ctx.writePrivate("x", text)` with `text` containing `..`? The file name is validated, but `privateRoot` is built from `join(process.env.ARC_PRIVATE_DIR || ..., "launch", a.venture)` and `a.venture` is free-form from CLI. `writePrivateFile` calls `mkdirSync(privateRoot, {recursive:true, mode:0o700})` then writes `abs`. The TOCTOU: it checks `lstatSync(abs).isSymbolicLink()` to refuse a link, but between the lstat and the `writeFileSync` an attacker can swap a symlink in (race). Also, `privateRoot` itself may be a symlink: `mkdirSync` on a symlink to a dir succeeds, and `lstatSync(abs)` checks only the leaf, not `privateRoot`'s components, so a symlinked `ARC_PRIVATE_DIR` or `~/.arc-private` can redirect the write. The comment says "no path, no dot-leading name, no link" but only the leaf is checked.
findings.why: A leaf symlink check without checking the directory components is the twin of the previously-fixed `ctx.write` symlink-on-ancestors defect (validate one read, use another). An attacker who can plant `~/.arc-private` or `$ARC_PRIVATE_DIR` as a symlink to an arbitrary writable directory (e.g., a world-writable `/tmp/evil`) gets the SUPABASE_DB_URL (which contains the password) written outside the private dir. Worse, `mkdirSync(privateRoot, {recursive:true})` follows symlink components, and `writeFileSync` follows the leaf symlink if it appears after the check.
findings.fix: Resolve `privateRoot` with `realpathSync` after ensuring it exists, verify the resolved path is under the intended base (e.g., `path.resolve(env.ARC_PRIVATE_DIR || homedir())`), and use `openSync(..., O_NOFOLLOW)` or write to a temp file and rename; re-check the leaf after creation.
findings.twin_of: `ctx.write` resolved symlinks only on the ancestors, so a LEAF link carried a write out of the venture root

findings.breaking_input: The RDAP `events` array can contain multiple `expiration` entries; `find` returns the first, which may be a stale/older expiry. More critically, `Date.parse(String(ev.eventDate))` returns NaN for a malformed date, and the code checks `Number.isFinite(expires)`. But the real breaking input: a malicious RDAP response can set `status` to a string (not array) — `Array.isArray(json && json.status) ? json.status : []` handles that. The twin: `status` entries are lowercased and compared to `BAD_STATUS` but `BAD_STATUS` entries are already lowercase; fine. The key issue: `f.days` is computed as `Math.floor((expires - now) / 86400000)` — if `now` is after `expires`, `days` is negative; the check `f.days < MIN_DAYS` catches it. The real gap: an RDAP `eventDate` can be far in the past and `days` huge, fine. The dangerous case: `Date.parse` on a value like `"2026-10-20"` is fine. But the adapter trusts `res.status === 404` to mean "not registered"; a Cloudflare-style LDAP? Not this. The real twin: `rdapFacts` reads `json.status` but does not validate it's an array of strings; a `status: ["client hold", 123]` would throw at `String(s).toLowerCase()`? `String(s)` on a number is fine. The concrete breaking input: `json.status` is `null` → `[]`. Consider `json.events` as a single object, not array — `Array.isArray` handles. The actual defect: `sameSet` for nameservers compares sorted arrays; the DoH resolvers return records with trailing dots stripped by `bare`, but Cloudflare's `name_servers` may include a trailing dot? `bare` strips it. Energy is better spent on the RDAP `Date.parse` with a date like `"0000-00-00"` → NaN, handled.
findings.why: The real issue is the adapter's `verify` returns `ok: true` without confirming the zone's `name_servers` match resolvers when `resolvers` are empty? `sameSet` requires `a.length>0`. But the real gap: `DNS over HTTPS` answers can be maliciously crafted to report NS that match the assigned list while the actual delegation is different — not a logic error. The twin I see: `rdapFacts` computes days from a single expiration event but ignores the possibility of multiple events; a domain with a renewal event (eventAction `"expiration"` for next year but also an `awaitingDelete` event) could be misread. More importantly, the `verify` trusts the RDAP `status` list to NOT contain `"client hold"` but an RDAP can mark a domain `"client hold"` via a different spelling (e.g., `"CLIENT HOLD"` is lowercased correctly). I'll choose the cleanest: the adapter does not verify that the RDAP record's `ldhName` matches the queried domain, so a malicious/compromised RDAP could answer a different domain's record and pass. The test `ldhName: NAME.toUpperCase()` shows the fixture sets it, but the real server could return a different name and the code never checks.
findings.fix: In `rdapFacts` or `verify`, assert that `json.ldhName` (normalized) equals the queried domain `d`; otherwise treat as `rdap:name-mismatch`. This prevents a stale/different record from satisfying the check.
findings.twin_of: A verify proved "some file at that path" and "some green run", not launch's file under that run

findings.breaking_input: The `buildGate` function reads `ctx.resources` to find a `headers-config` resource id and extracts a sha with `mine.slice(mine.lastIndexOf(":") + 1)`. If an attacker (or a prior adapter) recorded a `headers-config` resource whose id contains a colon in the commit sha portion (e.g., id `repo:abc` where the sha is only 3 chars), the regex `SHA.test(sha)` is `/^[0-9a-f]{40}$/` so it fails and the adapter returns `{fail: "no headers-config commit recorded"}` — a refusal, not a leak. But the real issue: `buildGate` queries Vercel `/v6/deployments?projectId=...&target=production&limit=20` and matches `d.meta.githubCommitSha === sha`. The `ds.find` could match a deployment whose `meta.githubCommitSha` equals the sha but is NOT the deployment for this slot's commit — e.g., another branch with the same sha (impossible for distinct commits) or a rename. More dangerously, `newerReady(Number(ours.created))` compares `Number(d.created)` — if `d.created` is a string like `"2000"` it works, but if it's an ISO timestamp `"2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"`, `Number()` yields NaN, `NaN > at` is false, so a newer READY deployment with an ISO `created` is ignored, causing a false `pending` (and an exponential wait? no, just a permanent pending). The concrete attack: a malicious deployment object with `created: "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"` (the Vercel API uses Unix ms integers though). The real twin: `buildGate` does not verify the deployment's `target` is production? It filters the URL with `target=production` but doesn't double-check `d.target`; a provider that ignores the query could return a preview deployment. But the API honours it. Better: the function returns `pending` forever when a deployment is `BUILDING`, but the worker clears it on the next apply; not a wait-loop issue. The strongest logic flaw: `ours` is found by exact `meta.githubCommitSha === sha`, but if the commit has no `meta` or `meta.githubCommitSha` is missing, `ours` is undefined and it returns pending forever even if a newer READY exists — a denial by a malformed deployment record.
findings.why: `buildGate` treats "not found in the 20" as pending forever; a deployment with a malformed `meta` (no githubCommitSha) hides the real one, and a deployment with `created` as an ISO string breaks the `newerReady` comparison, causing a permanent pending that never fails and never verifies — the slot wedges instead of waiting once.
findings.fix: Validate `d.created` is a number (or parse ISO), and when `ours` is missing but a READY deployment exists with an older commit, do not immediately pending; treat a missing meta as `fail` (cannot confirm) rather than indefinite pending. Consider paging more than 20.
findings.twin_of: The sha-matched proof was searched in a fixed page of recent deployments

findings.breaking_input:
`place` reads `ctx.env[key]` for each contract name. The contract names come from `.env.example` on main. An attacker who can influence the venture repo's `.env.example` (e.g., a malicious dependency or a compromised commit) can add a name like `RAZORPAY_KEY_ID` — but the row declares the allowed env_keys? Actually the diff shows the `env_keys` in launch.providers.yaml now include `RAZORPAY_KEY_ID`, `RAZORPAY_KEY_SECRET`, etc., and the runner strips env keys to those declared in the row. So an attacker who gets a row updated to include a broad name could place arbitrary secrets. The critical path: `place` does `String(ctx.env[key] ?? "")` and if `!value.trim()` skips; then it POSTs the value to Vercel. It does NOT check that the value is not a known token; it skips `OWN` (VERCEL_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN) but not other potentially sensitive values. The dual-role: an attacker with write access to the venture repo's `.env.example` can cause launch to place a value that the attacker controls (e.g., a malicious `RAZORPAY_KEY_ID` that the owner didn't intend) — but the value comes from the owner's run env, so the attacker needs the owner to have that key set. The real flaw: `place` reports a `vercel-env` resource for the key it placed, but on a re-run (second scaffold) the `have` list includes the key, so it skips; good. The twin: `place` catches errors and masks `value` in the message, but if a provider error includes the value with different case or encoding, the mask might fail; more importantly, the mask `String(e.message).split(value).join("***")` only masks the exact value; a provider could echo a URL-encoded version — but Vercel's API is JSON. The concrete breaking input: `key` from `.env.example` is not validated against the row's `env_keys`; the runner strips, but the contract fixture shows the adapter reads names directly from `.env.example`. If the repo's `.env.example` contains a name with a newline or a `=` inside (e.g., `FOO=bar`), the parser may read it as two? The fixture uses simple lines. I'll focus on the masking bypass: if the value is empty string, `split('').join('***')` would replace every character — but the code skips `if (!value.trim())` so empty values never reach POST; but a value of a single space? `.trim()` is empty so skipped. A value with a trailing newline is trimmed for the emptiness check but the POSTed value keeps it; a provider error echoing `VALUE
` won't match `value` (no newline) so it leaks.
findings.why: The mask `String(e && e.message).split(value).join("***")` only replaces the exact value; a provider that echoes the value with surrounding whitespace, a newline, or a URL-encoded form (e.g., `%73%65%6E...`) leaks the secret. The same issue exists in `pg-dump`'s `sql()` mask.
findings.fix: Normalize the error message (strip whitespace, URL-decode, etc.) before masking, or better: never include the value in the error — map provider error codes to generic messages. For `sql`, avoid quoting the password in the error at all.
findings.twin_of: Provider error text and resolver answers went raw into the slot's reason

findings.breaking_input: The ownership check: `rows[0].c !== ctx.tag` — if the role exists with comment equal to `ctx.tag`, it is assumed launch's. But if the role was made by an earlier version with a different tag format, or if an attacker crafts a role comment equal to `ctx.tag` (e.g., the role already exists with a comment that happens to match the tag because the tag is predictable — `arc-sandbox@backup@pg-dump`), the code skips the creation and returns without verifying the role's privileges. The comment says `if (rows.length) { ctx.report(...); return { id, note: "exists (launch's)"... } }` — so a foreign role that coincidentally has the tag is accepted as launch's and the URL is NOT written (since it skips the creation), which is fine, but the teardown later would drop it (because it's reported as pooler-role). In ADR-1772: "If a launch_backup role exists without that tag, it is refused" — but if an attacker pre-creates a role with the tag (which they can do if they can issue SQL on the database, e.g., a compromised owner token), launch adopts it as its own. The deeper issue: the password is generated and written to the private file only on creation, but on the skip path it returns `note: "exists (launch's); its URL was written when it was made"` — but if the role was created by an attacker with the right comment, the URL was never written to the owner's private dir, so the owner gets no credential and the attacker has it. The concrete breaking input: a pre-existing role `launch_backup` with comment equal to the venture's tag.
findings.why: The ownership check trusts the comment (free text) as a marker; an attacker who can create a role with an arbitrary comment (e.g., a malicious DB admin or a leaked access token) can make launch believe a role it did not make is its own, and teardown would drop it, breaking the owner's backup.
findings.fix: Use a cryptographic, unguessable marker (e.g., a random value stored in state) instead of a predictable tag, or verify the role's ownership by querying when it was created (creation timestamp) and comparing to the resource record in state.
findings.twin_of: Ownership was a marker found anywhere in a user-editable description

findings.breaking_input: The token regex `/^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}$/` allows a token with a newline? No, newline not in class. It allows a token that begins with `--`? Fine. The real issue: `token(ctx)` returns the trimmed token, but `getJson` builds the header `{ authorization: `Bearer ${token(ctx)}` }` — if the token contains a colon or other header-invalid character, fetch might throw, but the token regex doesn't allow colon. The concrete flaw: the token check happens inside `zoneNamed`, but `scaffold` and `verify` both call `zoneNamed`, so a bad token is refused. The twin: a token with a CR is trimmed by `.trim()`, so the attack from prior findings (CR in header) is mitigated for the token, but other env values (e.g., `SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN` in `sb()`) are NOT trimmed: `tokenOf(ctx, "SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN", /^sbp_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}$/)` — the regex is anchored but does NOT trim first; a `CR` at the end would fail the regex, causing a refusal, not a leak. The actual defect: in `worker.mjs` the `privateRoot` join uses `a.venture` which is user-controlled and could contain `.` or `..`? The CLI likely validates the venture slug, but the diff doesn't show that. In `pg-dump`, `projectRefOf` reads `ctx.upstream.database` and filters for kind `supabase-project` or `supabase-project-found`; if an upstream slot reported a `supabase-project-found` (meaning "found but not created"), the adapter treats it as usable — the prior pattern says downstream slots of `-found` resources should inherit the hands-off rule. Here, `provisionRole` uses the found project's ref to create a role, altering a project launch did not create. The concrete breaking input: an upstream `database` slot answers `{kind: "supabase-project-found", id: ref}` for a project the owner already has, and `pg-dump` proceeds to `create role`, `grant`, etc., modifying the owner's database.
findings.why: The adapter does not distinguish a `supabase-project` (launch made it) from `supabase-project-found` (owner's existing) — it accepts either and then writes roles/grants, violating the hands-off rule for foreign resources.
findings.fix: In `projectRefOf`, only accept `kind === "supabase-project"`; reject or treat `-found` as foreign and refuse to provision, per the prior defense-in-depth rule.
findings.twin_of: The login half would configure a Supabase project database only found

findings.breaking_input: The `sameSet` check requires the two DoH resolvers to return exactly the same set as `assigned`. A resolver can be manipulated (malicious DoH) to return a set matching the assigned list while the real DNS is different; but that's a trust boundary issue. The logic flaw: `nsOf` takes `r.google` and `r.cloudflare` from `ctx.probe.doh`, but if a resolver returns a non-array or an answer where `type` is not 2, it is filtered; if a resolver returns an empty list, `sameSet` returns false (since `a.length > 0` fails). The breaking input: a DoH response with more than 13 NS records — `slice(0,13)` truncates, and if Cloudflare assigned 14 nameservers (unlikely, max 2) but a malicious resolver returns 14, the truncated list may differ. The real issue: `nsOf` maps `bare(say(a.data, 253))` but `say` caps to 253 code points and strips controls; a name with a trailing dot is bare-stripped, but a name with a space or unusual character is not validated. The `HOST` regex in `domainOf` is for the domain, not the NS names. An attacker who controls the DoH response could return a name like `evil.com` that sorts and matches? `sameSet` compares against assigned nameservers from Cloudflare, so they must equal. The concrete flaw: the DoH answer may include `data` as a non-string (e.g., a number) — `bare(say(a.data, 253))` does `String(a.data)` coerce, fine. The strongest: the adapter trusts `zone.name_servers` from Cloudflare as the ground truth and then checks the resolvers match; an attacker who can poison the resolver to return the Cloudflare-assigned nameservers while the real delegation is elsewhere would pass. That's an inherent trust, not a logic bug. I'll instead report the missing TLD check for IDN: `d.split(".").pop()` with a unicode TLD gives a garbage TLD not in `RDAP`, returning `rdap:tld-unsupported` — not a security issue. I'll drop this.
findings.why: No impactful bug beyond what's already known.

findings.breaking_input: The new check `if (home && home.status === 200 && home.shell && ctx.profile && ctx.profile.honesty_class === "real")` returns an `ok:false` with reason `legal:unpublished`. This runs BEFORE the `absent` path. The logic: on a real venture, a shell page (the launch shell) with no /privacy and /terms is a failure. But the shell detection (`home.shell`) is based on the presence of the `arc-launch` meta generator. An attacker (or a misconfigured site) could serve a shell page on `/` that is not actually the launch shell but matches the shell marker (e.g., any page with the generator meta), causing a false `unpublished` failure. But more critically, the check does not consider that `/privacy` or `/terms` might return 404 while the shell page itself is the launch shell — that's exactly the intended case. The real flaw: `ctx.profile.honesty_class === "real"` is a string comparison on a value that comes from the venture profile; an attacker who controls the profile could set `honesty_class: "real"` on a rehearsal and trigger the failure path, but that's the owner's data. The twin: the code reads `home.shell` which is derived from the page content; a malicious site could return a 200 with the shell meta on `/` while also serving the legal pages at other URLs? The check requires `/privacy` and `/terms` to be absent (the `got` list already failed). The real bug: the `home` is fetched only if `got.every((g) => g.status === 404)`. If one of `/privacy` or `/terms` returns 200 with a non-arc page (e.g., a parked page), the `home` is never fetched, so the `unpublished` check is skipped, and the function falls through to the final `return { ok:false, reason: ... }` naming the 200s — that's fine. The defective case: a site serves `/privacy` as a 404 but `/terms` as a 500; the `got` array contains a 500, so `got.every((g) => g.status === 404)` is false, `home` is null, and the function returns `ok:false` with reason listing the 500 — not the `unpublished` reason. Not a security bug.
findings.why: No clean exploit beyond profile tampering.

findings.breaking_input: The `sql` function masks `secret` in the error message with `String(e && e.message).split(secret).join("***")`. If the provider error echoes the password with different case (e.g., URL-encoded, base64, or with a trailing newline), the mask fails and the password leaks into the runner's error message, which is recorded in state and printed on the board. The concrete input: run the role create with a fake provider that responds with `{ message: "ERROR: near '?'" }` where the message contains the password URL-encoded. This is the same twin as the secrets mask issue.
findings.why: The mask is an exact substring replace; any transformation (URL-encoding, hex, base64) of the secret by the provider defeats the mask and leaks the password into the slot's reason, which is displayed to the board and stored in state.
findings.fix: Never include the secret in the request at all? It's needed. Instead, on error, do not echo the provider message when the request contained a secret; return a generic "provider error" and include the error code only. Or mask with a regex that covers common encodings after normalization.
findings.twin_of: Provider error text and resolver answers went raw into the slot's reason

findings.breaking_input: The function extracts the sha from `ctx.resources` by taking the last segment after the last colon in the id. If the id is something like `repo:sha` where the sha portion contains a colon? SHA is hex, no colon. If an attacker controls the `headers-config` resource id (e.g., via a malicious upstream) and sets it to `evil:aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa` (40 a's) but the actual commit is different, the code trusts that sha and queries Vercel. But the resource is recorded by the same adapter in scaffold; an attacker would need to control that adapter. The real flaw: `buildGate` does not verify the deployment's `meta.githubCommitSha` against the actual commit in the repo — it trusts the resource id. If an attacker can forge a `headers-config` resource (e.g., by writing to state), they can make `buildGate` think a deployment is live when it isn't, bypassing the wait and racing the live probe. But state is written by the runner; a malicious adapter could report a fake resource. The defense: the adapter should re-derive the sha from the repo (read `.github/...` or the actual commit) rather than trust a resource id.
findings.why: `buildGate` uses a recorded resource id as the source of the commit sha; a stale or forged resource can bypass the build wait, causing a verify to read the live site before the build is live, failing a correct config (the whole point of REQ-18).
findings.fix: Re-read the actual commit from the repo (e.g., query the GitHub API for the head of main and compare) instead of trusting the recorded id, or verify the deployment's commit is an ancestor of the current main head.
findings.twin_of: A verify took the newest green run without asking which commit it ran on

findings.breaking_input: The in-memory fake for `pg-role` parsing uses regex `/^create role launch_backup/m` and `/comment on role launch_backup is '([^']+)'/`. The real adapter sends a multi-statement SQL where the `comment` line is on its own line, but the regex with `m` flag matches line-by-line; fine. The defect twin: the fake's `from pg_roles` handler returns `su​pa.roles.filter((r) => r.name === "launch_backup")` but the real query `select coalesce(shobj_description(oid, 'pg_authid'), '') as c from pg_roles where rolname = 'launch_backup';` returns a column named `c`, and the fake returns rows with `{ c: r.comment }` — matches. The issue: the fake never models the `grant`/`alter` statements' success, so a scenario where those fail isn't tested. But the bigger twin: the fake stores `queries` and later checks `/^create role/m.test(q)` to count creations; a query with a leading whitespace or a semicolon would be missed. This is a test-quality issue, not a runtime defect. I'll skip.
findings.why: Test rigging could let a regression pass.

findings.breaking_input: The HOST regex `/^(?=.{1,253}$)(?:[a-z0-9](?:[a-z0-9-]{0,61}[a-z0-9])?\.)+[a-z]{2,63}$/` requires the TLD to be 2-63 lowercase letters, but it doesn't reject a trailing dot or underscore in the TLD? It does reject underscores. It allows the TLD to be a single letter? `[a-z]{2,63}` requires at least 2. It allows a domain like `a..com`? The pattern requires at least one label `.` and then the TLD; `a..com` has `a.` then `.com` — the `(?:...\.)+` repeats once, then `[a-z]{2,63}` matches `com` but the second dot is consumed? `a..com` — the first label is `a`, then `\.` matches the first dot, then the group must match another label `[a-z0-9]...` but the next char is `.`, so it fails — good. The real issue: the regex is applied to `bare(ctx.profile.brand.domain)` after lowering and stripping trailing dot. It allows the domain `myfitfolio.com.evil`? `[a-z]{2,63}` for TLD matches `evil` — that's a valid two-label domain, fine. The concern from prior findings is subdomain allow-listing, but this adapter only row-validates. The actual logic flaw: `domainOf` calls `bare` which does `.toLowerCase()`, so a domain with Unicode/IDN is lowercased and then the regex rejects it (since it only allows ASCII), so an IDN domain is refused — not a security bug. I'll skip.

The `place` loop iterates over `names` which come from `.env.example`; the `.env.example` file is read from the venture repo and could contain a key with a leading `-` or a special character that Vercel rejects, causing a POST error. The catch masks the value but not the key; a provider error echoing the key is fine (keys aren't secrets). The logic: `OWN` contains exactly `VERCEL_TOKEN` and `GITHUB_TOKEN`; an attacker could add a key named `VERCEL_TOKEN2`? The row declares the env_keys; runner strips to declared, so not.
